$comment: Source of truth for the demo bookshelf. scripts/gen-example-pdfs.py draws each PDF and emits exact glyph geometry; scripts/build-examples.mjs assembles the self-contained readers + bookshelf from the built viewer bundle. Coordinates are PDF points (origin bottom-left, y up).

lines.text: Byte order decides how a multibyte integer is laid out in memory.
Big-endian stores the most significant byte at the lowest address.
Little-endian stores the least significant byte first, as x86 does.
Network protocols standardise on big-endian, called network order.
So htonl and ntohl convert between host order and that convention.
Serialising a struct with raw memcpy bakes in the writer's byte order.
A reader on the other endianness then decodes every field backwards.
The fix is an explicit wire format, not a mirror of process memory.

notes.body: **Big-endian** = most-significant byte first. Handy mnemonic: it reads left-to-right like we do. See [the next page](#page=2).
This is the actual bug: `memcpy` of a struct is *not* a portable wire format. Inline math works too, e.g. $2^{32}-1$.

lines.text: A published reading is a self-contained folder of static files.
It loads only local assets and never contacts a remote origin.
Drop it at any nested path on any static host and it just works.
Highlights sit on selected text; regions box a figure; points pin a spot.
The panel below is a region; the marker to its right is a point note.

notes.body: The core contract: **no runtime dependency** on the app domain or any CDN.
A **region note** boxes an area — use it for figures or scanned pages with no selectable text.
A **point note** pins a single spot.
